run.question: My AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 has high latency issues. Investigate why.

report.summary: The question names an AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1, but the only target this Run can read is a Kubernetes cluster (target_id m0-otel-20260909, source 'otel-demo') running the OpenTelemetry demo, and no AWS/CloudWatch data source is available in this Run, so no Lambda duration, init-duration, concurrency or Lambda log data could be read (runbook steps 1-5 could not be executed; the CloudWatch/CloudWatch Logs tool is missing). Nothing named 'payment-processor', 'lambda' or 'processor' exists among the cluster's pods, deployments or jobs; the only payment-related entity observed is a different one, the Kubernetes Deployment 'payment' in namespace otel-demo (image ghcr.io/open-telemetry/demo:2.0.2-payment), whose single pod payment-6f7bc865d6-9z92d is Running and Ready with restartCount 1, and whose sampled container logs from 2026-11-21T06:28:31Z to 06:57:38Z contain only info-level 'Charge request received.' / 'Transaction complete.' pairs with no error evidence. Its flagd-config ConfigMap declares payment fault flags (paymentFailure, paymentUnreachable) with defaultVariant 'off', and no runtime flag override was observable. Because the named Lambda is not observable here and both Prometheus and Jaeger returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE for every query, no latency cause for the named function can be established and no root cause is named.

claims.text: Rejected: that the AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 is represented in the registered target. Cluster-wide searches over pods (32 items processed) and deployments (24 items processed) for names matching 'payment|lambda|processor' returned only namespace otel-demo objects 'payment-6f7bc865d6-9z92d' and 'payment'; a jobs query (0 items processed) matched nothing, and namespaces present are default, kube-node-lease, kube-public, kube-system, local-path-storage, opspilot-readonly and otel-demo. The registered target is a Kubernetes/OTel-demo environment, not an AWS Lambda account.

The only payment-related workload observed in the cluster is Deployment 'payment' in namespace otel-demo (1 replica, 1 ready) running image ghcr.io/open-telemetry/demo:2.0.2-payment, with env FLAGD_HOST=flagd, FLAGD_PORT=8013, PAYMENT_PORT=8080 and OTEL_SERVICE_NAME taken from the label app.kubernetes.io/component; this is a Kubernetes Deployment, a different entity from an AWS Lambda function.

Pod payment-6f7bc865d6-9z92d (owned by ReplicaSet payment-6f7bc865d6) is phase Running, container 'payment' ready=true with restartCount 1; its previous container instance terminated at 2026-11-21T04:23:42Z with exitCode 255 and reason 'Unknown', and the current instance started 2026-11-21T04:23:48Z with the pod Ready condition last transitioning at 2026-11-21T04:23:49Z.

The newest 100 of 188 matching lines of the payment container's stdout (times 2026-11-21T06:28:31Z through 2026-11-21T06:57:38Z) are all pairs of level=info messages 'Charge request received.' and 'Transaction complete.' with trace_id/transactionId fields; the read shows no error, warn, timeout or exception line, and 88 earlier lines were not shown.

Counter-evidence to the otel-demo payment service failing during the sampled log window: in the payment container's own logs between 06:28:31Z and 06:57:38Z every 'Charge request received.' line is immediately followed by a matching 'Transaction complete.' line with the same trace_id and transactionId, and no error line was read; this sampling cannot clear the service for periods outside the sample or for its 88 omitted older lines.

ConfigMap 'flagd-config' in namespace otel-demo holds demo.flagd.json in which the fault-injection flags that name the payment service are declared with a non-failing default: paymentFailure ('Fail payment service charge requests n%') is state ENABLED with defaultVariant 'off' and variants 100%/90%/75%/50%/25%/10%/off, and paymentUnreachable ('Payment service is unavailable') is state ENABLED with defaultVariant 'off'. Other latency-relevant flags, such as imageSlowLoad (variants 10sec/5sec/off) and adManualGc, adHighCpu, kafkaQueueProblems, cartFailure, productCatalogFailure, recommendationCacheFailure, loadGeneratorFloodHomepage, are likewise defaultVariant 'off' in this file.

If the intended subject is the otel-demo 'payment' service rather than an AWS Lambda, then the declared payment fault flags are off by default and the sampled logs show completed charges, so fault injection through paymentFailure/paymentUnreachable is not supported as an explanation for latency in the observed sample; the variant actually in effect at runtime (flagd override) is not observable with these tools, so this remains a hypothesis and not a cleared finding.

The payment container's restart (previous instance exitCode 255 with reason 'Unknown' at 2026-11-21T04:23:42Z inside the authorized window) is a change on a different entity than the named Lambda; whether it was a node/containerd-level restart affecting many demo pods or something specific to payment was not established, so it is not treated as impact or as a cause here.

To answer the Lambda latency question, attach an AWS CloudWatch/CloudWatch Logs data source for us-east-1 and then follow the runbook against function 'payment-processor': Duration Average/Maximum and p95/p99 per 300s, InitDuration Average/Count for cold starts, ConcurrentExecutions Maximum per 60s versus the account concurrency limit, and log-group filter patterns '[ERROR] OR [WARN] OR timeout' plus a REPORT query for max(@maxMemoryUsed) vs @memorySize. Those five steps could not be carried out in this Run because no CloudWatch tool was available.

If the intended subject is actually the otel-demo 'payment' Kubernetes service, restore readability of the Prometheus and Jaeger data sources and then read payment's own signals: traces_span_metrics_calls_total{service_name="payment"} split by status_code, rpc_server_duration_milliseconds_bucket / rpc_client_duration_milliseconds_count for its gRPC Charge path, app_payment_transactions_total, and the http_server_request_duration_seconds_count latency for the checkout call path.

gaps: No AWS/CloudWatch integration is present in this Run's available data sources (only jaeger, knowledge, kubernetes, prometheus are available; not_integrated lists change_history). Therefore nothing about the Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 - Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, memory, error rate or its log group - could be queried, so the reported high latency could not be reproduced, measured or compared to a baseline.

The registered target's Prometheus data source returned status=error reason=SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE at 2026-11-21T06:57:49Z-06:57:55Z for get_metric_names (twice), execute_prometheus_instant_query and get_prometheus_target. All latency and error-rate metric series (traces_span_metrics_calls_total, rpc_server_duration_milliseconds_bucket, rpc_client_duration_milliseconds_count, app_payment_transactions_total, http_server_request_duration_seconds_count) are therefore unknown in this Run, not zero.

The Jaeger data source returned status=error reason=SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE at 2026-11-21T06:57:49Z and 06:57:51Z for traces_list_services, so no span, status-code or duration evidence for the payment service could be obtained and no call chain is claimed.

A cluster-wide events query over the authorized window returned status=no_data with 0 items (involvedObject grouping produced nothing), so no Kubernetes event evidence (restart reason, eviction, OOM, probe failure) is available for the payment pod restart at 2026-11-21T04:23:42Z.

Payment pod log coverage is partial: only the newest 100 of 188 matching lines were shown (88 omitted), the previous container instance produced no readable lines, and lines outside the container's retained stdout are unknown.

flagd runtime flag state (which variant was actually in effect during the window) is not observable with the available tools; only the demo.flagd.json declared defaults in ConfigMap flagd-config could be read.

Kubernetes objects read here are the cluster's state at query time (about 2026-11-21T06:57-06:58Z), not the state during the earlier part of the window, so they cannot show when the payment pod restarted or what the workload looked like at other times.

The Prometheus readiness of the cluster's own monitoring path was not established: pod prometheus-readonly-proxy-f4866f767-62bgn shows restartCount 3 in the pods listing, but its logs matched no line (status=no_data) and the cause of the Prometheus unavailability remains unknown.
next_steps: Provision an AWS CloudWatch (metrics + logs) integration for us-east-1 so function 'payment-processor' Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, Errors/Throttles and its REPORT/memory fields can be read and compared to a pre-incident baseline.

Confirm with the requester whether the subject is the AWS Lambda 'payment-processor' or the OpenTelemetry-demo service 'payment', since the only observable payment workload in this target is the Kubernetes Deployment 'payment' in namespace otel-demo.

If the otel-demo payment service is the subject, restore Prometheus and Jaeger access for target m0-otel-20260909 and then compare payment span error ratio and rpc_server_duration_milliseconds bucket distribution against an earlier baseline window before drawing any latency trend.
Check flagd's live flag state (not just the ConfigMap defaults) to confirm whether paymentFailure or paymentUnreachable was ever enabled during the window.

data.alertmanager.yml:
global: {}
receivers:
- name: opspilot
  webhook_configs:
  - http_config:
      authorization:
        [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL] /etc/alertmanager/opspilot/token
        type: Bearer [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL]: 0
    send_resolved: true
    url: http://opspilot-web:8080/intake/alertmanager
- name: opspilot-self
route:
  group_by:
  - alertname
  - namespace
  - service
  group_interval: 1m
  group_wait: 10s
  receiver: opspilot
  repeat_interval: 1h
  routes:
  - matchers:
    - opspilot_self="true"
    receiver: opspilot-self
templates: []

data.relay:
connectors:
  spanmetrics: {}
exporters:
  debug: {}
  opensearch:
    http:
      endpoint: http://opensearch:9200
      tls:
        insecure: true
    logs_index: otel
  otlp:
    endpoint: jaeger-collector:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true
  otlphttp/prometheus:
    auth:
      [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL] basicauth/prometheus
    endpoint: http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/otlp
    tls:
      insecure: true
extensions:
  basicauth/prometheus:
    client_auth:
      [REDACTED_CREDENTIAL] ${env:PROMETHEUS_COLLECTOR_PASSWORD}
      username: collector
  health_check:
    endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:13133
processors:
  batch: {}
  k8sattributes:
    extract:
      metadata:
      - k8s.namespace.name
      - k8s.deployment.name
      - k8s.statefulset.name
      - k8s.daemonset.name
      - k8s.cronjob.name
      - k8s.job.name
      - k8s.node.name
      - k8s.pod.name
      - k8s.pod.uid
      - k8s.pod.start_time
    passthrough: false
    pod_association:
    - sources:
      - from: resource_attribute
        name: k8s.pod.ip
    - sources:
      - from: resource_attribute
        name: k8s.pod.uid
    - sources:
      - from: connection
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 5s
    limit_percentage: 80
    spike_limit_percentage: 25
  resource:
    attributes:
    - action: insert
      from_attribute: k8s.pod.uid
      key: service.instance.id
  transform:
    error_mode: ignore
    trace_statements:
    - context: span
      statements:
      - replace_pattern(name, "\\?.*", "")
      - replace_match(name, "GET /api/products/*", "GET /api/products/{productId}")
receivers:
  httpcheck/frontend-proxy:
    targets:
    - endpoint: http://frontend-proxy:8080
  jaeger:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:14250
      thrift_compact:
        endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:6831
      thrift_http:
        endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:14268
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:4317
      http:
        cors:
          allowed_origins:
          - http://*
          - https://*
        endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:4318
  prometheus:
    config:
      scrape_configs:
      - job_name: opentelemetry-collector
        scrape_interval: 10s
        static_configs:
        - targets:
          - ${env:MY_POD_IP}:8888
  redis:
    collection_interval: 10s
    endpoint: valkey-cart:6379
  zipkin:
    endpoint: ${env:MY_POD_IP}:9411
service:
  extensions:
  - health_check
  - basicauth/prometheus
  pipelines:
    logs:
      exporters:
      - debug
      processors:
      - k8sattributes
      - memory_limiter
      - resource
      - batch
      receivers:
      - otlp
    metrics:
      exporters:
      - otlphttp/prometheus
      - debug
      processors:
      - k8sattributes
      - memory_limiter
      - resource
      - batch
      receivers:
      - httpcheck/frontend-proxy
      - redis
      - otlp
      - spanmetrics
    traces:
      exporters:
      - otlp
      - debug
      - spanmetrics
      processors:
      - k8sattributes
      - memory_limiter
      - resource
      - transform
      - batch
      receivers:
      - otlp
      - jaeger
      - zipkin
  telemetry:
    metrics:
      level: detailed
      readers:
      - periodic:
          exporter:
            otlp:
              endpoint: otel-collector:4318
              protocol: grpc
          interval: 10000
          timeout: 5000

content.name: lambda-performance-troubleshooting
content.content:
# AWS Lambda High Latency Troubleshooting

## Overview
This runbook helps diagnose and resolve AWS Lambda function performance issues including high latency, timeouts, and cold starts.

## Steps

### Step 1: Query Performance Metrics
Use CloudWatch to check Lambda function latency over time:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name Duration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 2: Check Function Logs
Look for errors or slow operations in CloudWatch Logs:
```bash
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --filter-pattern "[ERROR] OR [WARN] OR timeout" --limit 100
```

### Step 3: Analyze Cold Start Patterns
Query CloudWatch for cold start frequency:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name InitDuration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Count --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 4: Check Concurrent Executions
Verify Lambda isn't hitting concurrency limits:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name ConcurrentExecutions --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 60
```

### Step 5: Review Memory Utilization
Check if function needs more memory allocation:
```bash
aws logs insights start-query --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --start-time <epoch-start> --end-time <epoch-end> \
  --query-string "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @type = 'REPORT' | stats max(@maxMemoryUsed), avg(@memorySize)"
```
